title: Socrates Refuses to Arrest Leon of Salamis
text:
In 404 BC Athens lost the Peloponnesian War, and a Spartan-backed oligarchy, later called the Thirty Tyrants, took control of the city. The Thirty executed many of their opponents and seized the property of wealthy citizens and foreign residents.

They also tried to make as many Athenians as possible complicit in their crimes. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury at his trial in 399 BC what happened to him. The Thirty summoned him and four other men to the Tholos, their headquarters, and ordered them to go to Salamis and bring back Leon, a citizen they had decided to put to death.

The other four went to Salamis and brought Leon back, and he was executed. Socrates, by his own account, simply went home. He told the jury that he had shown, not in words but in action, that he did not care at all about death, but cared above all about doing nothing unjust or impious. He added that he might well have been killed for it, had the Thirty not fallen soon afterward.

In the same speech he recalled an earlier time, under the democracy, when he alone of the presiding committee had opposed an illegal trial.
lesson: Even when you cannot stop an injustice, you can refuse to take part in it. Quiet refusal is still a choice, and it counts.
people: Socrates, the Thirty Tyrants, Leon of Salamis
source: Plato, Apology 32b to 32e; Xenophon, Memorabilia, Book 4, chapter 4
